**Donda Clairann West** (née**Williams**; July 12, 1949 – November 10, 2007) was an American educator and chair of Chicago State University's Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater. She was best known for being the mother of American rapper Kanye West.

## Early life and career
[edit]
West was born and raised in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, the daughter of Lucille (née Eckles)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-1) and Portwood Williams Sr., a civil rights activist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-4) On August 19, 1958, she and her father took part in the Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-5) West attended Douglass High School, graduating in 1967.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-7) She earned her [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and her doctoral degree from Auburn University in 1980.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-oklahoman-8)
West began her teaching career in the early 1970s at Morris Brown College in Atlanta and began working at Chicago State University in 1980. West taught English at Nanjing University for a year as a scholar through the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program. In all, West spent 27 years at Chicago State, in head of the department of English, communications, media and theater. A statement from the university recalled West's role in establishing the university's Gwendolyn Brooks Center for Black Literature and Creative Writing "as an academic focus to teach writings of African-American authors and poets while fostering new literary talent."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-9)

## Early life and career
West raised Kanye in the Chicago area after leaving Atlanta, where she had lived along with her husband, Ray, from whom she separated when Kanye was 3.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-10) Although she strongly emphasized the importance of education to Kanye, she fully supported him when he decided to drop out of college to pursue a music career. In 2004, she retired from teaching and moved to California to work full-time for her son. She was often seen at his side at parties and award shows. She was also a firm defender of her son's controversial comments. West stated that she "trained her son for greatness." "There is no room for shyness. I raised him that way, to think critically and analytically and not be afraid to voice what you feel. I helped shape that. I think leaders are people who must do that."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-11) She was also chief executive of West Brands, the parent company of her son's businesses.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-12)

## Early life and career
West worked to address dropout and illiteracy rates, while partnering with community organizations to provide underprivileged youth access to music education.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-13) The Foundation's first initiative, Loop Dreams, challenged at-risk students to learn how to write and produce music while simultaneously improving their academic skills. In 2007, the foundation partnered with Strong American Schools as part of their "Ed in '08" campaign.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-15) In 2008, the foundation was renamed to the Dr. Donda West Foundation following her death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-16) The Dr. Donda West Foundation was committed to providing high-quality programs in partnership with community organizations such as Challengers Boys & Girls Club in South Central Los Angeles, California. The foundation ceased operations in 2011.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-17)
On November 10, 2007, Donda West died at age 58.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-18) In January 2008, the Los Angeles County coroner's office said that she had died of coronary artery disease and multiple post-operative factors from cosmetic surgery.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-19) Authorities in Los Angeles launched an investigation into her death after learning the doctor who operated on her, Jan Adams, had convictions for alcohol-related offenses and at least two major malpractice settlements.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-20)

## Early life and career
During Kanye's first concert following her funeral (performed at The O 2 Arena in London on November 22), he dedicated a performance of "Hey Mama", as well as a cover of Journey's "[Don't Stop Believin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Stop_Believin' "Don't Stop Believin'")," to his mother, and did so on all other dates of his Glow in the Dark Tour.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-21) She was posthumously featured and referenced on multiple songs in Kanye's 2021 namesake studio album for her, _Donda_.
California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger subsequently signed the "Donda West Law" in 2009. This legislation makes it mandatory for patients to receive medical clearance through a physical examination before undergoing elective cosmetic surgery.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-22)
West's memoir, _Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Star_, was published in 2009.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-23) West wrote in her book that she always wanted her son to go to college, but after witnessing his passion for hip hop and his talent producing beats, she later supported his decision to pursue music.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-24)

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
Before **Donda West** managed global brand portfolios or inspired studio albums, she was a dedicated scholar and educator. Her educational path was rooted in higher education and a commitment to Black literature and linguistics. After completing her foundational studies, she earned her EdD from Auburn University in 1980, solidifying her standing as a leader in English education.
Throughout her career, Dr. West demonstrated a passion for language, teaching, and cross-cultural communication. You can learn more about her family history and personal roots on her WikiTree family profile. She brought an energetic, student-first philosophy into every classroom she managed, showing how academic rigour and personal empathy go hand in hand.

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
### Civil Rights Activism and Early Education
Dr. West’s commitment to leadership took root early in her life. Born in Oklahoma City on July 12, 1949, she grew up in an environment where social action was part of daily family life. On August 19, 1958, at nine years old, she participated in the historic Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City. Organized by NAACP Youth Council leader Clara Luper, the demonstration was a early effort to desegregate public accommodations.
Donda participated alongside her father, Portwood Williams, a civil rights activist who drove the lead vehicle during the actions. Her childhood nickname was “Big Girl,” given affectionately by her father, who encouraged her early confidence.
These experiences shaped her worldview. She pursued higher education with focus, earning a Bachelor of Arts in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and later a Master’s degree from Atlanta University. These academic settings provided the springboard for her career in higher education.

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
### Donda West as Educator and Scholar at Chicago State
Dr. West spent 27 years at Chicago State University, serving as a professor and chair of the Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater before retiring in July 2004. During her tenure, she helped reshape the university’s literary focus, serving as a co-founder of the Gwendolyn Brooks Center for Black Literature and Creative Writing. The center became an important community hub for Black writers, scholars, and poets.
Her scholarly work extended internationally as well. As detailed in her Wikipedia entry, Dr. West served as a Fulbright U.S. Scholar, traveling to Nanjing, China, where she taught English at Nanjing University as a Foreign Expert. She also spent time early in her teaching career at Morris Brown College in Atlanta, where she chaired the English Department.
![Image 1: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
She believed in teaching students to think critically, express themselves without fear, and engage with literature as a tool for personal growth.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
![Image 2: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
When Kanye West broke into the music industry, his mother was his constant champion. While many parents might have balked at a child dropping out of college to pursue hip-hop production, Dr. West recognized her son’s drive and artistic potential. In July 2004, she retired from academia to step into the role of full-time general manager for her son, becoming the CEO of West Brands LLC.
In 2007, she published her book, _Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Superstar_, detailing her experiences balancing single motherhood, academic life, and raising an artist in Chicago.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
### How Donda West Shaped Kanye West’s Development
Dr. West’s supportive parenting style mixed discipline with encouragement. An early story from Kanye’s rise illustrates her dedication: during his early career, she rented a U-Haul van and personally drove him and his studio equipment from Chicago to Newark, New Jersey, so he could pursue production opportunities. Kanye later commemorated the road trip in his lyrics on “Touch the Sky.”
Dr. West also shared how she reacted upon first hearing his acclaimed debut album, _The College Dropout_. Sitting in a parked car, listening to the finished tracks, she broke down in tears of pride, wanting to roll down the windows and yell to passersby about her son’s work.
She often explained that her goal was never simply to raise a performer, but to teach him to think analytically and stand firmly behind his convictions—a trait that defined both mother and son.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
### Musical Tributes and the Donda Album
Kanye West frequently featured his mother as his central muse. His 2005 track “Hey Mama” served as a public thank-you for her sacrifices. After her sudden passing in November 2007, her absence heavily influenced his emotional tone and artistic focus on subsequent projects, notably _808s & Heartbreak_.
In August 2021, Kanye released his 10th studio album, titled _Donda_. The 27-track album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart and earned multiple nominations at the 64th Annual Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.
Dr. West’s voice appears on the album, providing spoken-word excerpts on the title track “Donda,” credited alongside choir vocals. Track details and streaming metadata are available on MusicBrainz.
The album’s opening track, “Donda Chant,” features repeating chants of her name, which fans and music theorists noted matches the rhythm of a beating heart. The broader cultural impact of the album and its live stadium listening events are documented on Wikipedia’s Donda overview.

## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
The tragic death of Dr. Donda West at age 58 sent shockwaves through the entertainment industry and prompted public discussions regarding elective surgery standards, post-operative care, and patient advocacy.

## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
### Surgical Complications and Investigation
On November 9, 2007, Dr. West underwent a five-and-a-half-hour elective procedure involving liposuction, a tummy tuck, and a breast reduction. The following day, November 10, she suffered sudden health complications at her home in Playa Del Rey, California. After experiencing a severe sore throat and chest tightness, she collapsed and was rushed to Centinela Freeman HealthSystem Marina Campus, where she was pronounced dead in the emergency room.
The Los Angeles County Coroner’s official investigation concluded that Dr. West died of heart disease while experiencing “multiple post-operative factors.” The report noted pre-existing coronary artery disease and noted there was no evidence of surgical or anesthetic misadventure during the operation itself.
Investigators pointed out that while she had been advised to receive recovery care at a specialized medical facility, she had opted to recover at home with family and caregivers. The absence of written home-care medical logs made it challenging for investigators to trace her exact vital signs during her final hours.

## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
### California’s Donda West Law and Patient Safety
The public coverage of Dr. West’s passing spurred immediate action by lawmakers seeking to improve patient safety during cosmetic procedures. In 2009, California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger signed into law State Assembly Bill 592, officially known as the **Donda West Law**.
![Image 3: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
The Donda West Law requires all patients undergoing elective cosmetic surgery in California to receive a thorough physical examination and formal medical clearance from a licensed physician before going under the knife. By mandating pre-surgery screenings, the legislation aims to identify hidden cardiovascular risks and prevent similar post-operative tragedies.

## Philanthropy, Creative Ventures, and Civic Honors
Throughout her life and in the years following her death, Dr. West’s impact has been preserved through community programs, creative collectives, and municipal tributes.

## Philanthropy, Creative Ventures, and Civic Honors
### Charitable Foundations and Youth Mentorship
Dr. West was deeply committed to community work and improving educational access for urban youth. Together with Kanye, she established the Kanye West Foundation, later renamed the Dr. Donda West Foundation.
One of its major initiatives was “Loop Dreams,” a program designed to engage at-risk youth by using music production technology to teach academic, math, and literacy skills. The initiative aimed to lower high school dropout rates by meeting students where their passions lay.
Although the foundation officially wound down operations in 2011, its blueprint inspired subsequent non-profit youth initiatives in Chicago, including Donda’s House (later rebranded as Artistry Youth Outreach), co-founded by artist Che “Rhymefest” Smith to offer arts instruction to young creatives.

**Donda Clairann West** (née**Williams**; July 12, 1949 – November 10, 2007) was an American educator and chair of Chicago State University's Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater. She was best known for being the mother of American rapper Kanye West.
texts.1:
## Early life and career
[edit]
West was born and raised in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, the daughter of Lucille (née Eckles)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-1) and Portwood Williams Sr., a civil rights activist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-4) On August 19, 1958, she and her father took part in the Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-5) West attended Douglass High School, graduating in 1967.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-7) She earned her [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and her doctoral degree from Auburn University in 1980.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-oklahoman-8)
West began her teaching career in the early 1970s at Morris Brown College in Atlanta and began working at Chicago State University in 1980. West taught English at Nanjing University for a year as a scholar through the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program. In all, West spent 27 years at Chicago State, in head of the department of English, communications, media and theater. A statement from the university recalled West's role in establishing the university's Gwendolyn Brooks Center for Black Literature and Creative Writing "as an academic focus to teach writings of African-American authors and poets while fostering new literary talent."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-9)
texts.2:
## Early life and career
West raised Kanye in the Chicago area after leaving Atlanta, where she had lived along with her husband, Ray, from whom she separated when Kanye was 3.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-10) Although she strongly emphasized the importance of education to Kanye, she fully supported him when he decided to drop out of college to pursue a music career. In 2004, she retired from teaching and moved to California to work full-time for her son. She was often seen at his side at parties and award shows. She was also a firm defender of her son's controversial comments. West stated that she "trained her son for greatness." "There is no room for shyness. I raised him that way, to think critically and analytically and not be afraid to voice what you feel. I helped shape that. I think leaders are people who must do that."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-11) She was also chief executive of West Brands, the parent company of her son's businesses.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-12)
texts.3:
## Early life and career
West worked to address dropout and illiteracy rates, while partnering with community organizations to provide underprivileged youth access to music education.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-13) The Foundation's first initiative, Loop Dreams, challenged at-risk students to learn how to write and produce music while simultaneously improving their academic skills. In 2007, the foundation partnered with Strong American Schools as part of their "Ed in '08" campaign.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-15) In 2008, the foundation was renamed to the Dr. Donda West Foundation following her death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-16) The Dr. Donda West Foundation was committed to providing high-quality programs in partnership with community organizations such as Challengers Boys & Girls Club in South Central Los Angeles, California. The foundation ceased operations in 2011.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-17)
On November 10, 2007, Donda West died at age 58.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-18) In January 2008, the Los Angeles County coroner's office said that she had died of coronary artery disease and multiple post-operative factors from cosmetic surgery.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-19) Authorities in Los Angeles launched an investigation into her death after learning the doctor who operated on her, Jan Adams, had convictions for alcohol-related offenses and at least two major malpractice settlements.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-20)

## Early life and career
During Kanye's first concert following her funeral (performed at The O 2 Arena in London on November 22), he dedicated a performance of "Hey Mama", as well as a cover of Journey's "[Don't Stop Believin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Stop_Believin' "Don't Stop Believin'")," to his mother, and did so on all other dates of his Glow in the Dark Tour.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-21) She was posthumously featured and referenced on multiple songs in Kanye's 2021 namesake studio album for her, _Donda_.
California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger subsequently signed the "Donda West Law" in 2009. This legislation makes it mandatory for patients to receive medical clearance through a physical examination before undergoing elective cosmetic surgery.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-22)
West's memoir, _Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Star_, was published in 2009.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-23) West wrote in her book that she always wanted her son to go to college, but after witnessing his passion for hip hop and his talent producing beats, she later supported his decision to pursue music.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-24)

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
Before **Donda West** managed global brand portfolios or inspired studio albums, she was a dedicated scholar and educator. Her educational path was rooted in higher education and a commitment to Black literature and linguistics. After completing her foundational studies, she earned her EdD from Auburn University in 1980, solidifying her standing as a leader in English education.
Throughout her career, Dr. West demonstrated a passion for language, teaching, and cross-cultural communication. You can learn more about her family history and personal roots on her WikiTree family profile. She brought an energetic, student-first philosophy into every classroom she managed, showing how academic rigour and personal empathy go hand in hand.

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
### Civil Rights Activism and Early Education
Dr. West’s commitment to leadership took root early in her life. Born in Oklahoma City on July 12, 1949, she grew up in an environment where social action was part of daily family life. On August 19, 1958, at nine years old, she participated in the historic Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City. Organized by NAACP Youth Council leader Clara Luper, the demonstration was a early effort to desegregate public accommodations.
Donda participated alongside her father, Portwood Williams, a civil rights activist who drove the lead vehicle during the actions. Her childhood nickname was “Big Girl,” given affectionately by her father, who encouraged her early confidence.
These experiences shaped her worldview. She pursued higher education with focus, earning a Bachelor of Arts in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and later a Master’s degree from Atlanta University. These academic settings provided the springboard for her career in higher education.

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West
### Donda West as Educator and Scholar at Chicago State
Dr. West spent 27 years at Chicago State University, serving as a professor and chair of the Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater before retiring in July 2004. During her tenure, she helped reshape the university’s literary focus, serving as a co-founder of the Gwendolyn Brooks Center for Black Literature and Creative Writing. The center became an important community hub for Black writers, scholars, and poets.
Her scholarly work extended internationally as well. As detailed in her Wikipedia entry, Dr. West served as a Fulbright U.S. Scholar, traveling to Nanjing, China, where she taught English at Nanjing University as a Foreign Expert. She also spent time early in her teaching career at Morris Brown College in Atlanta, where she chaired the English Department.
![Image 1: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
She believed in teaching students to think critically, express themselves without fear, and engage with literature as a tool for personal growth.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
![Image 2: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
When Kanye West broke into the music industry, his mother was his constant champion. While many parents might have balked at a child dropping out of college to pursue hip-hop production, Dr. West recognized her son’s drive and artistic potential. In July 2004, she retired from academia to step into the role of full-time general manager for her son, becoming the CEO of West Brands LLC.
In 2007, she published her book, _Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Superstar_, detailing her experiences balancing single motherhood, academic life, and raising an artist in Chicago.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
### How Donda West Shaped Kanye West’s Development
Dr. West’s supportive parenting style mixed discipline with encouragement. An early story from Kanye’s rise illustrates her dedication: during his early career, she rented a U-Haul van and personally drove him and his studio equipment from Chicago to Newark, New Jersey, so he could pursue production opportunities. Kanye later commemorated the road trip in his lyrics on “Touch the Sky.”
Dr. West also shared how she reacted upon first hearing his acclaimed debut album, _The College Dropout_. Sitting in a parked car, listening to the finished tracks, she broke down in tears of pride, wanting to roll down the windows and yell to passersby about her son’s work.
She often explained that her goal was never simply to raise a performer, but to teach him to think analytically and stand firmly behind his convictions—a trait that defined both mother and son.

## Influence on Kanye West and Musical Legacy
### Musical Tributes and the Donda Album
Kanye West frequently featured his mother as his central muse. His 2005 track “Hey Mama” served as a public thank-you for her sacrifices. After her sudden passing in November 2007, her absence heavily influenced his emotional tone and artistic focus on subsequent projects, notably _808s & Heartbreak_.
In August 2021, Kanye released his 10th studio album, titled _Donda_. The 27-track album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart and earned multiple nominations at the 64th Annual Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.
Dr. West’s voice appears on the album, providing spoken-word excerpts on the title track “Donda,” credited alongside choir vocals. Track details and streaming metadata are available on MusicBrainz.
The album’s opening track, “Donda Chant,” features repeating chants of her name, which fans and music theorists noted matches the rhythm of a beating heart. The broader cultural impact of the album and its live stadium listening events are documented on Wikipedia’s Donda overview.
texts.6:
## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
The tragic death of Dr. Donda West at age 58 sent shockwaves through the entertainment industry and prompted public discussions regarding elective surgery standards, post-operative care, and patient advocacy.
texts.7:
## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
### Surgical Complications and Investigation
On November 9, 2007, Dr. West underwent a five-and-a-half-hour elective procedure involving liposuction, a tummy tuck, and a breast reduction. The following day, November 10, she suffered sudden health complications at her home in Playa Del Rey, California. After experiencing a severe sore throat and chest tightness, she collapsed and was rushed to Centinela Freeman HealthSystem Marina Campus, where she was pronounced dead in the emergency room.
The Los Angeles County Coroner’s official investigation concluded that Dr. West died of heart disease while experiencing “multiple post-operative factors.” The report noted pre-existing coronary artery disease and noted there was no evidence of surgical or anesthetic misadventure during the operation itself.
Investigators pointed out that while she had been advised to receive recovery care at a specialized medical facility, she had opted to recover at home with family and caregivers. The absence of written home-care medical logs made it challenging for investigators to trace her exact vital signs during her final hours.
texts.8:
## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
### California’s Donda West Law and Patient Safety
The public coverage of Dr. West’s passing spurred immediate action by lawmakers seeking to improve patient safety during cosmetic procedures. In 2009, California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger signed into law State Assembly Bill 592, officially known as the **Donda West Law**.
![Image 3: Picture of Christopher Pape](blob:http://localhost/e8a57f4972516a1d3218894eabc89576)
The Donda West Law requires all patients undergoing elective cosmetic surgery in California to receive a thorough physical examination and formal medical clearance from a licensed physician before going under the knife. By mandating pre-surgery screenings, the legislation aims to identify hidden cardiovascular risks and prevent similar post-operative tragedies.
texts.9:
## Philanthropy, Creative Ventures, and Civic Honors
Throughout her life and in the years following her death, Dr. West’s impact has been preserved through community programs, creative collectives, and municipal tributes.
texts.10:
## Philanthropy, Creative Ventures, and Civic Honors
### Charitable Foundations and Youth Mentorship
Dr. West was deeply committed to community work and improving educational access for urban youth. Together with Kanye, she established the Kanye West Foundation, later renamed the Dr. Donda West Foundation.
One of its major initiatives was “Loop Dreams,” a program designed to engage at-risk youth by using music production technology to teach academic, math, and literacy skills. The initiative aimed to lower high school dropout rates by meeting students where their passions lay.
Although the foundation officially wound down operations in 2011, its blueprint inspired subsequent non-profit youth initiatives in Chicago, including Donda’s House (later rebranded as Artistry Youth Outreach), co-founded by artist Che “Rhymefest” Smith to offer arts instruction to young creatives.

**Donda Clairann West** (née**Williams**; July 12, 1949 – November 10, 2007) was an American educator and chair of Chicago State University's Department of English, Communications, Media, and Theater. She was best known for being the mother of American rapper Kanye West.

## Early life and career
[edit]
West was born and raised in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, the daughter of Lucille (née Eckles)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-1) and Portwood Williams Sr., a civil rights activist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-4) On August 19, 1958, she and her father took part in the Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-5) West attended Douglass High School, graduating in 1967.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-7) She earned her [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and her doctoral degree from Auburn University in 1980.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-oklahoman-8)
West began her teaching career in the early 1970s at Morris Brown College in Atlanta and began working at Chicago State University in 1980. West taught English at Nanjing University for a year as a scholar through the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program. In all, West spent 27 years at Chicago State, in head of the department of English, communications, media and theater. A statement from the university recalled West's role in establishing the university's Gwendolyn Brooks Center for Black Literature and Creative Writing "as an academic focus to teach writings of African-American authors and poets while fostering new literary talent."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-9)

## Early life and career
West raised Kanye in the Chicago area after leaving Atlanta, where she had lived along with her husband, Ray, from whom she separated when Kanye was 3.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-10) Although she strongly emphasized the importance of education to Kanye, she fully supported him when he decided to drop out of college to pursue a music career. In 2004, she retired from teaching and moved to California to work full-time for her son. She was often seen at his side at parties and award shows. She was also a firm defender of her son's controversial comments. West stated that she "trained her son for greatness." "There is no room for shyness. I raised him that way, to think critically and analytically and not be afraid to voice what you feel. I helped shape that. I think leaders are people who must do that."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-11) She was also chief executive of West Brands, the parent company of her son's businesses.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-12)

## Early life and career
West worked to address dropout and illiteracy rates, while partnering with community organizations to provide underprivileged youth access to music education.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-13) The Foundation's first initiative, Loop Dreams, challenged at-risk students to learn how to write and produce music while simultaneously improving their academic skills. In 2007, the foundation partnered with Strong American Schools as part of their "Ed in '08" campaign.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-15) In 2008, the foundation was renamed to the Dr. Donda West Foundation following her death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-16) The Dr. Donda West Foundation was committed to providing high-quality programs in partnership with community organizations such as Challengers Boys & Girls Club in South Central Los Angeles, California. The foundation ceased operations in 2011.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-17)
On November 10, 2007, Donda West died at age 58.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-18) In January 2008, the Los Angeles County coroner's office said that she had died of coronary artery disease and multiple post-operative factors from cosmetic surgery.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-19) Authorities in Los Angeles launched an investigation into her death after learning the doctor who operated on her, Jan Adams, had convictions for alcohol-related offenses and at least two major malpractice settlements.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-20)

## Early life and career
During Kanye's first concert following her funeral (performed at The O 2 Arena in London on November 22), he dedicated a performance of "Hey Mama", as well as a cover of Journey's "[Don't Stop Believin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Stop_Believin' "Don't Stop Believin'")," to his mother, and did so on all other dates of his Glow in the Dark Tour.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-21) She was posthumously featured and referenced on multiple songs in Kanye's 2021 namesake studio album for her, _Donda_.
California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger subsequently signed the "Donda West Law" in 2009. This legislation makes it mandatory for patients to receive medical clearance through a physical examination before undergoing elective cosmetic surgery.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-22)
West's memoir, _Raising Kanye: Life Lessons from the Mother of a Hip-Hop Star_, was published in 2009.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-23) West wrote in her book that she always wanted her son to go to college, but after witnessing his passion for hip hop and his talent producing beats, she later supported his decision to pursue music.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donda_West#cite_note-24)

### Civil Rights Activism and Early Education
Dr. West’s commitment to leadership took root early in her life. Born in Oklahoma City on July 12, 1949, she grew up in an environment where social action was part of daily family life. On August 19, 1958, at nine years old, she participated in the historic Katz Drug Store sit-in in Oklahoma City. Organized by NAACP Youth Council leader Clara Luper, the demonstration was a early effort to desegregate public accommodations.
Donda participated alongside her father, Portwood Williams, a civil rights activist who drove the lead vehicle during the actions. Her childhood nickname was “Big Girl,” given affectionately by her father, who encouraged her early confidence.
These experiences shaped her worldview. She pursued higher education with focus, earning a Bachelor of Arts in English from Virginia Union University in 1971 and later a Master’s degree from Atlanta University. These academic settings provided the springboard for her career in higher education.

## Early Career and Academic Distinction of Donda West

## Circumstances of Her Death and Legislative Impact
### Surgical Complications and Investigation
On November 9, 2007, Dr. West underwent a five-and-a-half-hour elective procedure involving liposuction, a tummy tuck, and a breast reduction. The following day, November 10, she suffered sudden health complications at her home in Playa Del Rey, California. After experiencing a severe sore throat and chest tightness, she collapsed and was rushed to Centinela Freeman HealthSystem Marina Campus, where she was pronounced dead in the emergency room.
The Los Angeles County Coroner’s official investigation concluded that Dr. West died of heart disease while experiencing “multiple post-operative factors.” The report noted pre-existing coronary artery disease and noted there was no evidence of surgical or anesthetic misadventure during the operation itself.

**Maria Owings Shriver** ( _SHRY-vər_; born November 6, 1955)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-1) is an American writer and journalist. Shriver is a member of the Shriver family and Kennedy family, a former First Lady of California, and the founder of the non-profit organization The Women's Alzheimer's Movement.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-3) She was married to actor and former Governor of California, Arnold Schwarzenegger, with whom she had four children, before separating in 2011 and divorcing in 2021.

Shriver began her journalism career at KYW-TV and briefly anchored the _CBS Morning News_ before joining NBC News in 1986. After anchoring weekend editions of the _Today_ show and the _NBC Nightly News_, she became a correspondent for _Dateline NBC_, also covering politics. After leaving NBC News in 2004 to focus on her role as First Lady of California, she returned in 2013 as a special anchor. For her reporting at NBC, Shriver received a Peabody Award in 1998 and was co-anchor for NBC's Emmy-winning coverage of the 1988 Summer Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-4) As executive producer of _The Alzheimer's Project_, Shriver earned two Emmy Awards and an Academy of Television Arts & Sciences award for developing a "television show with a conscience".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-5)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Shriver was born in Chicago, Illinois, on November 6, 1955, the second child and only daughter of politician Sargent Shriver and activist Eunice Kennedy. She is a niece of the late U.S. president John F. Kennedy, U.S. attorney general and U.S. senatorRobert F. Kennedy, U.S. senator Ted Kennedy, and six other siblings. A Roman Catholic,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-6) she is of mostly Irish and German descent.
Shriver spent her middle school years living in Paris[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-7) and returned permanently from France to Bethesda, Maryland, in 1970,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-sargent-8) where she attended Stone Ridge School of the Sacred Heart high school and graduated in 1973,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-10) later attending Manhattanville College in Purchase, New York, for two years, then transferring for a Bachelor of Arts degree in American studies at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., graduating in June 1977._[citation needed_]
Shriver began her journalism career with KYW-TV in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, she co-anchored _The CBS Morning News_ with Forrest Sawyer from August 1985 until August 1986, co-anchored NBC News's _Sunday Today_ from 1987 until 1990. Shriver also served as Saturday anchor 1989 & Sunday 1990 and contributing anchor 1996-1999 of _NBC Nightly News_. She was a contributing anchor on _Dateline NBC_ from 1992 until 2004. In August 2003, Shriver took an unpaid leave of absence from NBC News when her husband became a candidate in the 2003 California gubernatorial recall election._[citation needed_]

## Early life and education
Following her husband's November 17, 2003, inauguration as the 38th Governor of California, she became the First Lady of California. She then returned to reporting, making two more appearances for _Dateline NBC_. She left NBC News in February 2004.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-11)
She appeared as herself in the film _Last Action Hero_ (1993). She also played a minor role as herself in "Be Prepared", a 2006 episode of the television series _[That's So Raven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_So\_Raven "That's So Raven")_ promoting a "Preparedness Plan".
Shriver announced that she would not return to the news media after the excessive media coverage of the death of Anna Nicole Smith.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-13) Shriver subsequently returned to the news media.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-USA_Today-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-Mediabistro-15)
Video 3
Shriver, in 2019, talking about the inaugural meeting of the California Alzheimer's Task Force, which she chairs.

## Early life and education
In 2003, Shriver's father, Sargent Shriver, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, and she became an advocate and fundraiser for Alzheimer's patient care and biomedical research.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-AlzOrgProfile-16) Shriver was the executive producer of _The Alzheimer's Project_, a four-part documentary series that premiered on HBO in May 2009[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-17) and later earned two Emmy Awards.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-18) The series took a close look at cutting-edge research being done in the country's leading Alzheimer's laboratories. The documentary also examined the effects of this disease on patients and families. One of the Emmy Award-winning films, _Grandpa, Do you Know Who I Am?_ is based on Shriver's best-selling children's book dealing with Alzheimer's.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-19)

## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
In May 2009, Shriver planted the first edible garden at a state capitol in what once was a flower bed. She teamed up with Alice Waters on the project.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-69) The food grown in the organic garden is distributed to local food banks.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-70) Shriver has been an advocate for edible gardens and chairs the California School Garden Network that has doubled the number of gardens in state schools from 3,000 to 6,000 since 2004.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-71)
On April 30, 2013, NBC announced that Shriver would join the network again as a special anchor working on issues surrounding the shifting roles of women in American life.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-USA_Today-14)
On October 18, 2013, Shriver returned to the anchor desk on _Today_, filling-in for Savannah Guthrie for the first time since 1998 as co-anchor with Matt Lauer.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-Mediabistro-15)
She was one of the executive producers of _Still Alice_ (2014).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-72)

Jackson.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-73)

(L-R) Lynda Johnson Robb, Shriver, and Luci Baines Johnson at the Civil Rights Exhibit at the LBJ Presidential Library in 2014

## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
In 1977, Tom Brokaw introduced Maria to Austrian bodybuilder and actor Arnold Schwarzenegger at a charity tennis tournament being held at her mother's home. She married Schwarzenegger on April 26, 1986, in Hyannis, Massachusetts, at St. Francis Xavier Roman Catholic Church.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-74) They have four children; two daughters and two sons, including Katherine and Patrick.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-77)
On May 9, 2011, Schwarzenegger and Shriver announced their separation after 25 years of marriage, and Shriver moved out of the couple's Brentwood mansion.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-80) In a message for her Twitter followers posted on May 13, 2011, Shriver said: "Thank you all for the kindness, support and compassion. I am humbled by the love. Thank you."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-81)

## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
On May 17, 2011, Schwarzenegger publicly admitted to fathering Joseph Baena with longtime household staff member Mildred "Patty" Baena. Baena became pregnant in 1997, before his election as Governor of California.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-82) He confessed to Shriver only after she confronted him with the information, and after Shriver had confirmed her long-held suspicions in a conversation with Patty Baena.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-83) Shriver described Schwarzenegger's admission as "painful and heartbreaking". She declined to speak further on the issue, saying: "As a mother, my concern is for the children. I ask for compassion, respect and privacy as my children and I try to rebuild our lives and heal."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-84) Shriver filed for divorce on July 1, 2011, citing "irreconcilable differences".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-85) Due to various legal disputes, the divorce was not finalized until December 2021.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-86)
As executive producer of _The Alzheimer's Project_, Shriver earned two Emmy Awards and an Academy of Television Arts & Sciences award for developing a "television show with a conscience".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-87) She has additionally won Peabody Awards for her television journalism.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-88)
In 2009, Shriver was honored with the Shinnyo-en Foundation's 2009 Pathfinders to Peace Award, which is bestowed annually to a person who exemplifies the ideals of compassion, harmony, and peace.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-89)

## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
The [Saint John's Health Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_John's_Health_Center "Saint John's Health Center") has a nursery named after Shriver.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-90)
A hybrid rose was named after Shriver in October 2004. The Maria Shriver rose contains starchy-white blooms and a powerful citrus fragrance.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-91)
In 2017, the [Alzheimer's Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alzheimer's_Association "Alzheimer's Association") awarded Shriver with its first-ever Lifetime Achievement Award.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-92)

Maria Shriver Details "Pain and Prison" of Arnold Schwarzenegger Marriage
This is **Maria Shriver**'s total recall of her marriage to ex-husband **Arnold Schwarzenegger**.
The former First Lady of California got candid about her decades-long romance with the _Terminator_ star, detailing how it went from love at first sight during a 1977 tennis tournament to heartbreak upon learning his affair with the family housekeeper **Mildred Baena** in 2011.
"He smiled, laughed, looked you up and down," she wrote in a poem titled "At First Love" from her memoir _I Am Maria_. "It happened before you knew / And then you did / It would take you from there to here / From love and freedom / To pain and prison."
"It all happened at first sight / You fell / Fell hard / You would never ever really be able to reclaim your eyes / Or your heart," Maria continued. "Your eyes have never been the same nor will they ever be / Your heart open then broken."
In another poem titled "Time Stood Still," the 69-year-old seemingly alluded to the moment Arnold, 77, confessed tofathering son **Joseph Baena**, 27, with Mildred.
"I heard the words / But I had dissolved I wasn't there," wrote Maria, who shares kids **Katherine Schwarzenegger Pratt**, 35,**Christina Schwarzenegger**, 33,**Patrick Schwarzenegger**, 31, and**Christopher Schwarzenegger**, 27, with Arnold. "The moment changed everything / Nothing was ever the same again."
After all, as Maria noted, "I had been with Arnold since I was twenty-one years old—my entire adult life."
“As for me, the feelings I felt at the end of my marriage are hard to put into words," she shared in another chapter. "I was consumed with grief and wracked with confusion, anger, fear, sadness, and anxiety. I felt emotionally bereft and disconnected from life as I knew it."

Reed Saxon-Pool/Getty Images

**Maria Owings Shriver** ( _SHRY-vər_; born November 6, 1955)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-1) is an American writer and journalist. Shriver is a member of the Shriver family and Kennedy family, a former First Lady of California, and the founder of the non-profit organization The Women's Alzheimer's Movement.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-3) She was married to actor and former Governor of California, Arnold Schwarzenegger, with whom she had four children, before separating in 2011 and divorcing in 2021.
texts.1: Shriver began her journalism career at KYW-TV and briefly anchored the _CBS Morning News_ before joining NBC News in 1986. After anchoring weekend editions of the _Today_ show and the _NBC Nightly News_, she became a correspondent for _Dateline NBC_, also covering politics. After leaving NBC News in 2004 to focus on her role as First Lady of California, she returned in 2013 as a special anchor. For her reporting at NBC, Shriver received a Peabody Award in 1998 and was co-anchor for NBC's Emmy-winning coverage of the 1988 Summer Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-4) As executive producer of _The Alzheimer's Project_, Shriver earned two Emmy Awards and an Academy of Television Arts & Sciences award for developing a "television show with a conscience".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-5)

## Early life and education
[edit]
Shriver was born in Chicago, Illinois, on November 6, 1955, the second child and only daughter of politician Sargent Shriver and activist Eunice Kennedy. She is a niece of the late U.S. president John F. Kennedy, U.S. attorney general and U.S. senatorRobert F. Kennedy, U.S. senator Ted Kennedy, and six other siblings. A Roman Catholic,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-6) she is of mostly Irish and German descent.
Shriver spent her middle school years living in Paris[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-7) and returned permanently from France to Bethesda, Maryland, in 1970,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-sargent-8) where she attended Stone Ridge School of the Sacred Heart high school and graduated in 1973,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-10) later attending Manhattanville College in Purchase, New York, for two years, then transferring for a Bachelor of Arts degree in American studies at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., graduating in June 1977._[citation needed_]
Shriver began her journalism career with KYW-TV in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, she co-anchored _The CBS Morning News_ with Forrest Sawyer from August 1985 until August 1986, co-anchored NBC News's _Sunday Today_ from 1987 until 1990. Shriver also served as Saturday anchor 1989 & Sunday 1990 and contributing anchor 1996-1999 of _NBC Nightly News_. She was a contributing anchor on _Dateline NBC_ from 1992 until 2004. In August 2003, Shriver took an unpaid leave of absence from NBC News when her husband became a candidate in the 2003 California gubernatorial recall election._[citation needed_]

She appeared as herself in the film _Last Action Hero_ (1993). She also played a minor role as herself in "Be Prepared", a 2006 episode of the television series _[That's So Raven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_So\_Raven "That's So Raven")_ promoting a "Preparedness Plan".

## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
In 1977, Tom Brokaw introduced Maria to Austrian bodybuilder and actor Arnold Schwarzenegger at a charity tennis tournament being held at her mother's home. She married Schwarzenegger on April 26, 1986, in Hyannis, Massachusetts, at St. Francis Xavier Roman Catholic Church.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-74) They have four children; two daughters and two sons, including Katherine and Patrick.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-77)
On May 9, 2011, Schwarzenegger and Shriver announced their separation after 25 years of marriage, and Shriver moved out of the couple's Brentwood mansion.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-80) In a message for her Twitter followers posted on May 13, 2011, Shriver said: "Thank you all for the kindness, support and compassion. texts.16:
## First Lady of California (2003-2011)
On May 17, 2011, Schwarzenegger publicly admitted to fathering Joseph Baena with longtime household staff member Mildred "Patty" Baena. Baena became pregnant in 1997, before his election as Governor of California.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-82) He confessed to Shriver only after she confronted him with the information, and after Shriver had confirmed her long-held suspicions in a conversation with Patty Baena.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-83) Shriver described Schwarzenegger's admission as "painful and heartbreaking". She declined to speak further on the issue, saying: "As a mother, my concern is for the children. I ask for compassion, respect and privacy as my children and I try to rebuild our lives and heal."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-84) Shriver filed for divorce on July 1, 2011, citing "irreconcilable differences".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-85) Due to various legal disputes, the divorce was not finalized until December 2021.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-86)

In 2009, Shriver was honored with the Shinnyo-en Foundation's 2009 Pathfinders to Peace Award, which is bestowed annually to a person who exemplifies the ideals of compassion, harmony, and peace.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Shriver#cite_note-89)

Shriver began her journalism career at KYW-TV and briefly anchored the _CBS Morning News_ before joining NBC News in 1986. This is **Maria Shriver**'s total recall of her marriage to ex-husband **Arnold Schwarzenegger**.
The former First Lady of California got candid about her decades-long romance with the _Terminator_ star, detailing how it went from love at first sight during a 1977 tennis tournament to heartbreak upon learning his affair with the family housekeeper **Mildred Baena** in 2011.
"He smiled, laughed, looked you up and down," she wrote in a poem titled "At First Love" from her memoir _I Am Maria_. "It happened before you knew / And then you did / It would take you from there to here / From love and freedom / To pain and prison."
"It all happened at first sight / You fell / Fell hard / You would never ever really be able to reclaim your eyes / Or your heart," Maria continued. "Your eyes have never been the same nor will they ever be / Your heart open then broken."
In another poem titled "Time Stood Still," the 69-year-old seemingly alluded to the moment Arnold, 77, confessed tofathering son **Joseph Baena**, 27, with Mildred.

"The moment changed everything / Nothing was ever the same again."
After all, as Maria noted, "I had been with Arnold since I was twenty-one years old—my entire adult life."
“As for me, the feelings I felt at the end of my marriage are hard to put into words," she shared in another chapter. "I was consumed with grief and wracked with confusion, anger, fear, sadness, and anxiety. I felt emotionally bereft and disconnected from life as I knew it."

Reed Saxon-Pool/Getty Images

"I was unsure now of who I was, where I belonged, or who I belonged to," she explained. "Honestly, it was brutal, and I was terrified."
But eventually, Maria found her voice again. In a poem titled "Letting Go," she wrote of moving forward from her divorce with the _Total Recall_ actor, "He was the last to go and the hardest to let go of."

She added, "I loved you all in different ways / I know you loved me too in different ways / And so I release you / You are free and finally so am I / I let go."
